<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par155 />in poetic style, the attributive relation is expressed by simple co-ordination.<ref>The old view that all these cases arise from the ''omission'' of {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} is incorrect. These co-ordinated attributive clauses are rather a mere subdivision of the various kinds of circumstantial clauses (see § 156) which may be attached to a {{GHGterm|nomen regens}}. Cf. in English ''this is the letter'' (which) ''he wrote to me''.</ref>

{{GHGmargin-letter|155|c}}
The governing substantive or pronoun is frequently (in certain cases ''always'') resumed by a pronominal suffix or an adverb. The resumption may, however, be omitted, just as in relative clauses introduced by {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}}, &c.; see {{GHGpar|138|f}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|155|d}}
In Arabic a distinction is made between relative clauses used for the nearer definition of a ''determinate'' substantive (''ṣila''), and those which are attached to an ''indeterminate'' substantive (''ṣifa''). The former must be introduced by the demonstrative pronoun ''allaḏî'', the latter are always simply co-ordinated. The same distinction was no doubt originally observed in Hebrew, since simply co-ordinated relative clauses are most commonly found after ''indeterminate'' substantives (see the examples below), and in cases like {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=28|verse=49}} ({{GHGheb|text=גּוֹי אֲשֶׁר לֹֽא־תִשְׁמַע לְשֹׁנוֹ|translate=a nation whose tongue thou shalt not understand}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=66|verse=13}}, and especially {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=3|verse=11}}), the addition of {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} is explained from the special stress laid on the indeterminate substantive,<ref>So Baumann, op. cit., p. 14 f., following Böttcher, ''Lehrbuch'', ii. 80.</ref> ''a nation of such a kind, thou understandest not their tongue''. On the other hand, in poetic style at least, {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} is somewhat frequently omitted even after a determinate noun, but only rarely in prose (except by the Chronicler; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=9|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=12|verse=23|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=29|verse=1|hidebook=1}} (read prob. {{GHGheb|text=אֲשֶׁר}} for {{GHGheb|text=אֶחַד}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=15|verse=11}}; after {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=29|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=18|verse=23}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=30|verse=17|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=31|verse=19|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ezr|chapter=1|verse=5}}, but also {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=39|verse=4}}; for further instances, see Driver, {{GHGcite|title=Introd.}}<sup>8</sup>, p. 537, no. 30); so {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=18|verse=20}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=8|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=20|verse=15|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=13|verse=12}} (=which way), so {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=3|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=18|verse=23}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Neh|chapter=13|verse=23}}; after a pronominal subject, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=6|verse=9}}. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=52|verse=12}} for {{GHGheb|text=עָמַד}} read {{GHGheb|text=עֹמֵד}} with the LXX.

{{GHGmargin-letter|155|e}}
'''2.''' If the nearer definition of a substantive or pronoun is effected by simple co-ordination of the relative clause, it may take the form—

(''a'') Of a noun-clause, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=20|verse=21}} ''a man of the hill country of Ephraim'' {{GHGheb|text=שֶׁ֫בַע שְׁמוֹ|translate=whose name was Sheba}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=6|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=1|verse=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=3|verse=15|hidebook=1}} ''with princes'' {{GHGheb|text=זָהָב לָהֶם|translate=that had gold}}; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=11|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=22|verse=11}}; when referring to a noun-suffix, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=49|verse=14}} {{GHGheb|text=זֶה דַרְכָּם כֵּ֫סֶל לָ֫סוֹ|translate=this is the way of them who have}} (self-)''confidence''.—On periphrases of this kind to express negative attributes, as in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=38|verse=26}} {{GHGheb|text=עַל־אֶ֫רֶץ לֹא־אִישׁ|translate=on a land}} where ''no man'' is, see {{GHGpar|152|u}}, and cf. for this very short form of the relative clause, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=15|verse=13}} {{GHGheb|text=בְּאֶ֫רֶץ לֹא לָהֶם|translate=in a land}} that belongs ''not to them''; {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=32|verse=17}} ({{GHGheb|text=לַשֵּׁדִים לֹא אֱלֹהַּ}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Hb|chapter=1|verse=6}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=26|verse=17}} ({{GHGheb|text=לֹא־לוֹ}}).

{{GHGmargin-letter|155|f}}
(''b'') Of a verbal clause.

Here we must distinguish the cases in which the retrospective pronoun—
